 Early Social Security Claims Jumped 13% Amid Agency Turmoil, Locking Retirees Into Smaller Checks as Part B Climbs
 Published Nov 19, 2026 11:26 AM EST 
 By
 Elena Vega 
 SHVETS production | Pexels 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 The number of Americans filing new claims for Social Security retirement benefits rose by 267,000, or 13%, from October 2024 to April 2025 compared with the year before, according to an Urban Institute analysis described by KFF Health News . Typical year-to-year changes run about 2% to 3%.
 Retirement researchers link the jump to turmoil at the Social Security Administration during that period, including staff cuts, threatened field office closures, and public claims of widespread fraud. Claims then dropped by 235,000, or about 10%, from October 2025 to April 2026.
 The spike matters for health as much as for retirement income. People who claim early lock in a smaller monthly check for life, and that same check is where Medicare premiums are usually deducted and where many older adults find the money for prescriptions, copays, and other medical bills.
 A Spike Researchers Tied to Fear
 The analysis was led by Jack Smalligan, a senior policy fellow at the Urban Institute, who found that population growth and technical adjustments did not explain the size of the increase. He described the later decline as "almost an exact reversal" of the surge.
 Alicia Munnell, former director of the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, described the 2025 period as chaotic. A 2021 study from the center found that people shown fear-inducing headlines said they would claim benefits about a year earlier than people shown neutral ones.
 A Social Security spokesperson told KFF Health News that the agency has provided the best customer service in its history. The agency did not respond to questions about the reasons for the spike.
 For those who claimed during the surge, the reduction in their checks is generally permanent.
 The Lifetime Cost of Claiming at 62
 The penalty for claiming early is steep. For people born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67. Claiming at 62 cuts a retirement benefit by 30%, so a $1,000 benefit becomes $700, according to the Social Security Administration . A spouse's benefit claimed at 62 is cut by 35%.
 Waiting has the opposite effect. Benefits grow by about 8% for each year a person delays past full retirement age, up to age 70. One Delaware retiree profiled by KFF Health News said claiming at 64 cost him about $5,000 a year in income.
 There is also a coverage gap many people overlook. Claiming Social Security at 62 does not bring Medicare. Most people are not eligible for Medicare until 65 , so early claimers who leave a job with health benefits must find other coverage, such as a marketplace plan or a spouse's policy, for up to three years.
 Smaller Checks Meet Rising Medicare Costs
 Medicare costs are climbing. The standard Part B premium will be $209.40 a month in 2027, up $6.50, and the annual Part B deductible rises to $292, FedSmith reported from the CMS announcement. For most retirees, that premium comes straight out of their Social Security payment.
 A smaller check means the premium takes a larger share. In MedicalDaily's calculation, a person entitled to $2,000 a month at full retirement age who claims at 62 would receive about $1,400. The 2027 Part B premium would take about 15% of that check, compared with about 10.5% of the full benefit.
 Yearly raises are smaller in dollars, too. The 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 would add about $50 a month to a $1,400 check, compared with about $72 on a $2,000 check, and the Part B increase takes back $6.50 of either raise. A New York retiree profiled by KFF Health News said claiming early cost her about $300 a month.
 That squeeze can affect health decisions. Older adults on fixed incomes may face trade-offs among premiums, drug copays, dental care, and hearing aids, which traditional Medicare largely does not cover. MedicalDaily earlier examined how the Part B increase could shrink the Social Security raise for typical households.
 Long-term uncertainty adds pressure, and it is part of what drove anxious claiming in the first place. Without action by Congress, the retirement trust fund is projected to be depleted by late 2032, after which benefits could be cut by up to 22%.
 Who Feels the Squeeze, and Where to Get Help
 The people most exposed are those who claimed early without other savings, people with chronic conditions that bring steady medical bills, and widows or widowers who rely on a single check. Women, who tend to live longer, spend more years living on a reduced benefit.
 Help exists for people with limited income. Medicare Savings Programs, run by each state , can pay the Part B premium and, for some people, deductibles and coinsurance. People who qualify for Extra Help can pay less for prescription drugs . State Health Insurance Assistance Programs offer free, unbiased counseling on Medicare costs.
 People who are still deciding when to claim can review their estimates through a my Social Security account before filing. The agency allows people to withdraw a retirement application within 12 months of first becoming entitled, but they must repay the benefits they received.
 No single claiming age fits everyone. Health, savings, work plans, and marriage all matter, and a financial adviser or a free counselor can help weigh the trade-offs. MedicalDaily will report on new Social Security data and any changes to Medicare costs before benefits adjust in January.

 Key Questions Answered
 How much did early Social Security claims rise? By 267,000, or 13%, from October 2024 to April 2025 compared with the previous year.
 Why did claims jump? Researchers link it to turmoil at the Social Security Administration, including staff cuts, office closure threats, and fraud claims.
 How much smaller is a benefit claimed at 62? For people with a full retirement age of 67, the benefit is reduced by 30%.
 Does claiming Social Security early give me Medicare? No. Most people do not become eligible for Medicare until 65.
 How much is the 2027 Part B premium? $209.40 a month, with a $292 annual deductible.
 Where can retirees get help with Medicare costs? Medicare Savings Programs, Extra Help for drug costs, and free counseling through State Health Insurance Assistance Programs.
